subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: run an experiment by asking for a change [Action]
passage:
I almost handed in my notice last year, and I'm glad I didn't. I'm Pradeep. I was bored on a project that had no end in sight. Instead of quitting, I asked my manager Farhan for something specific: a different project, and clear goals for two months. He raised his eyebrows, but he said yes.

For eight weeks I watched myself like a scientist. Was I learning more? Did my mornings feel different? By week three I was sleeping better. By week six I'd shipped something I was proud of, and by the end I knew I wanted to stay. If nothing had changed, I'd have had real evidence to take away with me. Either way, it beat guessing.

qa.q: What did Pradeep ask Farhan for?
qa.a: A different project, and clear goals for two months.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling about the old project?
qa.a: Pradeep was bored and restless on a project with no end in sight, which had pushed the thought of resigning.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do if the two months showed no improvement, and why?
qa.a: Pradeep could then take the evidence to Farhan and begin planning a real move, because the trial answered the question honestly.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel about Pradeep's request?
qa.a: Farhan raised his eyebrows at first, so he may have been surprised, though agreeing shows he preferred keeping a good engineer to losing one.

grounding: The employee asks for a different project and clearer goals for two months and observes whether the work improves.

subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: run an experiment by asking for a change [Action]
passage:
I'm Arnab, and I sat beside Pallavi at the design studio for most of last year. By September she barely spoke in stand-ups, and I thought she'd hand in her notice any day.
Instead, one morning she booked twenty minutes with our lead. Later she showed me the email she'd sent after: "As discussed: for October and November I'll move to the signage project. Goals: finish two layouts a month, one review every Friday. We'll check on 30 November if this works."
For two months I watched. She took the signage files home once or twice. On Fridays she came out of reviews either frowning or grinning, never blank like before.
On 30 November she came back from the check-in and said, "Better. Not perfect. I'm staying till summer at least." I can't say exactly what changed inside her, but she started speaking in stand-ups again.

qa.q: On what date did Pallavi plan to check whether the change worked?
qa.a: She planned to check on 30 November.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have been feeling in September, before she asked for the change?
qa.a: She may have felt flat and discouraged, barely speaking in stand-ups, which made Arnab expect her to resign.

qa.q: Which other approach could Pallavi combine with this trial?
qa.a: She could keep a simple weekly note of what she enjoyed or disliked, so the 30 November check rests on clear evidence, not memory.

qa.q: How did Pallavi's trial look from Arnab's desk?
qa.a: Arnab saw her go from blank and silent to frowning or grinning after reviews, and speaking in stand-ups again, though Arnab can't know her full thoughts.

grounding: Shows an employee asking for a different project and clear goals for two months and watching whether work improves before deciding to leave.

subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist

passage:
1 March. Santosh had drafted his resignation twice. Instead, he walked into his manager Dhruv's cabin at the logistics firm. "I'm not happy on the invoicing work. Can I try the route-planning team for two months, with clear targets? Then we both see."
Dhruv thought for a moment. "Two months. You'll cut one route's delivery time and document the method. We review on 30 April."
18 March. Santosh stayed late, not from dread but because the route maps were a puzzle he wanted to crack. He noted each week what went well and what didn't in a small notebook.
30 April. The review. One route was faster, the documentation was patchy. Dhruv said so plainly. Santosh left the cabin thinking. The work felt better; the pace still didn't suit him. He decided to stay in route planning and ask for a mentor, and tore up the old resignation draft.

qa.q: On what date did Santosh and Dhruv review the trial?
How was Santosh feeling on 18 March compared with before?
qa.a: He felt curious and engaged, staying late because the route maps were a puzzle, not out of dread.

qa.q: What else could Santosh ask for to make the next stage work?
qa.a: He could ask for help with documentation along with a mentor, since the review showed that was the weak part.

qa.q: How does the trial look from Dhruv's side?
qa.a: Dhruv gets a motivated team member and clear results to judge, and can give honest feedback instead of losing Santosh to a sudden resignation.

grounding: Shows an employee asking for a different project and clear goals for two months and using the results to decide instead of quitting at once.
